title: Exide Industries mulls lead acid expansion to cash in on ‘sweet spot’ – Batteries International
content: Indian battery giant Exide Industries is considering further expansion of its lead acid battery manufacturing capacity to take advantage of a demand “sweet spot” in the sector. CEO and MD Avik Roy said the market was witnessing a unique sweet spot for lead acid because demand from both original equipment manufacturers (OEM) and the aftermarket was growing concurrently. “In the past, it never used to happen like this,” Roy told an earnings conference call on November 5. Previously, if the OEM was growing, the aftermarket would be slow and vice-versa, Roy said. Exide’s observations are in line with global analysis which has identified growth in both sectors, citing OEM demand being driven by rising factory-fit EV production, while aftermarket demand is driven by predictable replacement cycles of 12V and auxiliary batteries, even as EV fleets expand. Roy said: “Now we see both the segments growing strongly concurrently, we are investing capital in de-bottlenecking each of our factories. Thankfully, we have multiple factories where brown-field expansion and brown-field de-bottlenecking is possible. So we are doing that. “Substantial capital has been allocated to squeeze out every line, every asset.” Roy said the company was discussing additional capacity after approaches by a number of automotive OEMs that have announced their own capacity expansions including to cater for conventional internal combustion engines. “Since the automotive OEM market is growing, and we already had a very high market share — close to 60% in automotive OEM — we are growing along with the growth of the market.” This helps in two ways, giving a favourable mix as the trade business to OEM business ratio remains robust. Secondly, it helps the company in allocating capacity to markets where margins are higher. Batteries International has reported previously that Exide planned to invest more than Rs1,000 crore ($116 million) across its lead acid and lithium battery manufacturing businesses in the 2026 financial year, which ends on March 31, 2027 in India. title: Former EnerSys exec Schmitlein joins SiliconJoule as CFO – Batteries International
content: Mike Schmitlein has been appointed CFO of bi-polar lead battery developer SiliconJoule effective November 1. Schmitlein brings more than 25 years of leadership in the energy storage industry including at EnerSys, where he held several senior posts including working as CFO for 12 years up to his retirement in 2022. SiliconJoule said Schmitlein had joined during a period of rapid technical and market expansion. The company is scaling supply chains for its treated silicon wafers, industrialising assembly processes, and planning three new products to complement its core deep-cycling 24V GC2+ battery platform As CFO, Schmitlein will help guide the company’s upcoming private funding round, hopefully to be anchored by strategic investors SiliconJoule CEO Ray Kubis said: “Having worked with Mike in the past, I know firsthand the depth of skill and operational expertise he brings to the table. “As we scale our advanced battery technology, his financial discipline and deep industry insight will allow him to hit the ground running.” Schmitlein said many companies had tried to commercialise bi-pole battery technology. “This technology offers a genuine competitive alternative to lithium ion and other emerging chemistries across multiple applications.” Silicon Joule emerged in March 2026 from the rebranded company Gridtential formed over a decade before that. The new company name derived from the proprietary battery tech that uses treated silicon wafers as a structural and electrochemical component within advanced bipolar battery designs, including the new GC2+. content: India has reportedly banned exports of lithium ion battery black mass in a move aimed at strengthening domestic recycling capabilities to recover critical minerals. The government’s Directorate General of Foreign Trade announced the ban on November 11, according to reports by media organisations including the Press Trust of India (PTI). The Directorate General, part of the commerce and industry ministry, said India depends substantially on imports for a number of minerals and the ban will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, reducing the need for imports. According to the directorate, part of the commerce and industry ministry, while the country’s capacity to recycle battery waste and refine critical minerals has grown considerably, it is not being fully utilised due to inadequate feedstock availability. Exports of black mass generated in India divert this valuable secondary resource abroad, and domestic recyclers have, in some cases, had to import material to meet their requirements. Recycling battery waste is among the quickest and most sustainable ways of developing a domestic supply of these resources to power the nation’s electric mobility, advanced chemistry cell batteries, energy storage, electronics and renewable energy, the directorate said. The directorate has yet to respond to a Batteries International request for details of the ban and an estimate of the quantity of black mass involved. Meanwhile, India has been urged to introduce tighter regulation of battery dealers, mandatory reporting of spent battery collections and regular audits of authorised recycling facilities. The call came from L Pugazhenthy, executive director of the India Lead Zinc Development Association, at the 10th International Secondary Lead Conference in Colombo last month. title: China sets target for ‘new-type ESS’ boom by 2030 – Batteries International
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 规划目标
政策分类依据: 发改委、能源局发布2030年新型储能3亿千瓦装机及时长约3小时的量化目标与任务时间表
content: China has announced plans to speed-up development of new types of energy storage up to 2030, with a target of 300 million kilowatts of installed storage by 2030. The plans, issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration, were confirmed by China’s state Xinhua news agency on November 14. New types of ESS facilities will need to have an average storage duration of about three hours, according to the plans, which also aim to shift the sector from large-scale expansion to market-driven growth. According to Xinhua, new types of energy storage refer to energy storage technologies other than pumped-storage hydropower, mainly including electrochemical, compressed-air and gravity storage. The plans call for new types of energy storage to participate fairly in electricity markets, and encourage renewable energy megabases equipped with storage to join cross-provincial power markets as a single entity. In addition, the plans call for a refined pricing mechanism that reflects the value of stored power, with charging and discharging prices set through fair market trading. Xinhua cited research from Huayuan Securities noting that the emphasis on market mechanisms comes as China’s power market increasingly matures. Investment in new types of energy storage was initially policy-driven, relying largely on mandatory deployment rules and subsidies, but the sector is now shifting toward market-based mechanisms. Xu Dongjie, deputy chief engineer of the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute, said the 300-million-kilowatt target was a prudent, science-based minimum target that meets system needs and supports a reasonable rise in utilisation while giving the industry confidence and preventing investment-driven boom-and-bust cycles. According to the National Energy Administration, China leads the world in new types of energy storage, with installed capacity accounting for around 40% of the global total. By the end of 2025, China had built and put into operation 136 million kilowatts of new types of energy storage, with average storage duration reaching 2.58 hours ― 0.3 hours longer than at the end of 2024. title: BMW powers up battery supply chain with new Samsung and LG agreements – Batteries International
content: Germany’s BMW Group has signed high-voltage battery cell supply deals with South Korean battery makers Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution. BMW said on November 9 the agreements expands its portfolio of existing manufacturers and diversifies the auto giant’s Gen 6 high-voltage battery supply chain. Financial details and production capacities of the latest deals were not disclosed. BMW said Samsung and LG will supply from their manufacturing plants in Europe and the US respectively from the late 2020s onwards. BMW said the agreements underline its commitment to relying on local cell production in close geographical proximity to its high-voltage battery and vehicle production facilities. The auto company says the Gen 6 battery is based on the nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistry used in its Gen 5 battery system. Gen 6 introduces a new round cell format with direct cell-to-pack integration that is said to allow for greater energy density, reduced weight and more efficient use of space. Nicolai Martin, member of the BMW board of management responsible for the purchasing and supplier network said: “We aim to ensure our products’ global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets. To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets.” Batteries International reported earlier this year that BMW and Chinese battery major CATL had agreed to strengthen work on pilot projects and collaborate on cross-border data exchange in relation to the EU’s Battery Passport scheme. CATL and BMW have been working together on areas including battery production and R&D since 2012. title: BCI launches call for Amplify Award contenders for 2027 – Batteries International
content: Battery Council International has launched a call for applications for its prestigious BCI Amplify Award, which recognises highly effective and top-rated campaigns, programmes or communications that serve to inform, educate and promote the battery industry. Submissions for the 2027 Amplify Awards, to be presented at the BCI 2027 Convention + Power Mart Expo in Arizona, should be made by March 1, 2027. There are two categories of Amplify Awards — the award for product marketing and the industry leadership award. A list of potential campaigns and projects to consider for submissions have been posted on BCI’s web site. Clarios was announced as the latest winner of the Amplify Award for product marketing earlier this year, for the relaunch of its Autobatteries.com website as a consumer education resource. Baterias Moura won the Amplify Award for industry leadership for its video campaign highlighting the company’s support for its workers, its community, and a circular economy for lead batteries. content: Australian Vanadium (AVL) has secured a funding deal with the state of Western Australia to support the design, construction and commissioning of the company’s first proposed relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility. AVL said a grant up to a maximum of A$15 million ($10 million), awarded under the state’s Investment Attraction Fund, will enable it to deploy its proprietary V-NOMAD electrolyte production technology platform. The funding represents up to 50% of the project cost, with AVL responsible for meeting the balance of the project’s cost. The facility is planned to provide high-capacity electrolyte manufacturing capable of supporting gigawatt-hour scale vanadium flow battery projects. AVL said the move will be a material expansion of its existing electrolyte manufacturing capability. V-NOMAD has been independently developed by the company as a relocatable manufacturing facility to be co-located with VFB energy storage systems to reduce electrolyte costs. CEO Graham Arvidson said the grant was an important milestone for AVL and recognised the progress made in developing vanadium electrolyte manufacturing capability in Western Australia. In October 2026, AVL announced the signing of a non-binding memorandum of understanding to cooperate with US-based advanced battery tech firm Tyfast Energy on vanadium oxide products. The MOU established a framework for technical qualification and evaluation of future demonstration and commercial opportunities using AVL’s planned vanadium oxide products in Tyfast’s proprietary lithium vanadium oxide (LVO) anode technology. title: Veolia unveils ‘7,000-tonne black mass capacity’ plant in France – Batteries International
content: Veolia has launched a new plant in France to extract metals from EV batteries aimed at reducing exports of materials vital to Europe’s industrial sovereignty. The French multinational group said on November 12 the facility, in France’s Grand Est region, uses proprietary hydrometallurgical technology and has the capacity to process nearly 7,000 tonnes of black mass annually — which the firm said is equivalent to around usage for 20,000 tonnes of batteries. The amount of recycled metals, however, cannot make a real impact on Europe’s needs for raw materials for at least a decade. The process can recover more than 90% of the cobalt, nickel and copper contained in the feedstock, Veolia said. Feedstock for the plant will initially come from facilities in France, the UK and Switzerland, with recovered metals destined to supply European automotive, construction and defence markets. Veolia said recovering strategic metals such as nickel and cobalt is a major issue of competitiveness and sovereignty for Europe. CEO Estelle Brachlianoff said: “Through its technologies and pioneering expertise, Veolia is helping to create a sovereign supply of strategic metals from recycling. Thanks to this facility, where European black mass flows converge, this extraordinary resource can be recovered within Europe, today serving the metallurgy sector and, tomorrow perhaps, producing new European batteries.” European Commission EVP Stéphane Séjourné said: “For too long, Europe has watched its strategic raw materials leave the continent, only to import finished products from elsewhere. We must break free from this cycle of dependency.” Batteries International reported in October 2026 that the EU had rolled out 46 new projects in its latest scramble to secure raw materials critical to battery manufacturing and other industries to counter China’s “weaponisation” of the sector. The European Commission announced extraction processing and recycling projects for lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite and other materials — with others outside the EU to be unveiled later. content: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development has signed a €50 million ($55 million) deal to finance a new solar power plant integrated with Tunisia’s first utility-scale BESS. The bank said on November 12 it had approved the financing package with utility Société Tunisienne de l’Electricité et du Gaz (STEG) ― comprising a €30 million EBRD sovereign-guaranteed loan to STEG, complemented by a €20 million concessional loan from the Climate Investment Funds’ Clean Technology Fund (CTF). Under the Global Energy Storage Program, the CTF’s concessional financing makes the investment more affordable, and supports the deployment of battery storage technology in Tunisia. The project, located in Beni Mhira, includes a 50MWac solar photovoltaic plant integrated with a 10MW / 20MWh BESS. It will also include a 1.2km high-voltage transmission line connecting the facility to the national grid. STEG said the project is part of its wider programme to develop 380MWac of solar generation capacity and 100MWh of battery storage, in support of Tunisia’s efforts to diversify its energy mix and reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels. Aida Sitdikova, the bank’s director of sustainable infrastructure for the Middle East and Africa, said: “This first utility-scale battery is an important milestone for Tunisia’s energy security and its energy transition. title: Tianneng hails bid to become battery supplier for UN procurement support – Batteries International
content: China’s Tianneng Group has welcomed a recommendation that is set to see the battery maker become a UN-recognised supplier of products for new energy procurement projects. Tianneng, whose subsidiaries include lead acid battery manufacturing, said it was one of around 10 companies recommended to help new energy firms expand globally with UN procurement support. The announcement came on November 10 during a conference in Shanghai to discuss the global expansion and international procurement of new energy products. If confirmed, Tianneng would become part of the UN Procurement Catalog, which comprises details of goods and services that can be procured through the official UN system. In Shanghai, Tianneng showcased its multi-chemistry battery portfolio which also features lithium, sodium ion and solid-state batteries. Applications range from light vehicles, including electric two- and three-wheelers, to energy storage systems for homes, commercial and industrial users, AI data centres and utility-scale projects. Zhang Tianren, chairman of the Tianneng Group and chairman of the Global Battery and Energy Storage Council, told the conference the global energy transition was at a critical juncture. He said Tianneng’s inclusion in the UN procurement core supplier pool would affirm the group’s 40-year commitment to quality and innovation. “We will focus on better batteries and deeper system solutions, advancing R&D, local manufacturing and rooted branding to help drive the industry toward a more sustainable future. “The battery and energy storage industry must respond to uncertainty with more open standards alignment, deeper localised deployment and more resilient supply chains.” Batteries International reported in September 2026 that a Tianneng subsidiary had agreed outline proposals for cooperation and investment in battery manufacturing and energy storage projects in Egypt with Egyptian multinational the Mansour Group. The memorandum of understanding covered a study of opportunities to produce lead acid and lithium batteries for EVs, according to Egypt’s State Information Service. title: High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine
content:
Electric Heavy Machinery
autonomous
Jo Borrás
| Nov 15 2026 - 7:02 am PT
Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution:
fully self-driving haul trucks
Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.
“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”
That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.
Eacon conducts the ORCASTRA
Screencap; via EACON.
SANY has been working with Perth,
Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors
, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.
“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”
The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.
Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines
, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.
SANY SKT105ED
SANY delivered 200 haul trucks in August.
While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant)
the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain
, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.
Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

title: China's electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range
content:
Electric airplanes
Fred Lambert
| Nov 15 2026 - 6:43 am PT
COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.
It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.
The CE-25A: 19 seats, 10 fans, 400 km
The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.
The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.
The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.
The CATL connection
The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft,
as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit
CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.
~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.
How it compares
COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.
Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.
Heart is the closest Western comparison. It
dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022
, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range,
with BAE Systems working on the battery
. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.
Electrek’s Take
For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.
Look at trucking.
Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September
, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.
Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.
And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.
China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

title: Seven major engineering challenges stand between humans and a permanent Moon base
content: Returning astronauts to the Moon is one challenge. Keeping them there for months or years is another. A permanent lunar base will need much more than a landing vehicle and a pressurized habitat. It will require reliable power, locally sourced resources, radiation protection, autonomous construction systems, and infrastructure that can survive one of the harshest environments in the solar system. NASA’s plans for a sustained lunar presence near the South Pole highlight how much work remains. The agency is developing technologies for surface power, resource extraction, construction, communications, and dust mitigation, but many still need to be demonstrated and integrated under actual lunar conditions. Here are seven technologies that will be essential to turning the Moon from a destination for short missions into a place where humans can live and work for the long term. 1. Continuous power systems that survive the lunar night Solar panels are an obvious source of electricity on the Moon, but they cannot provide uninterrupted power everywhere. A lunar day and night each last approximately 14 Earth days, and locations in permanent shadow receive little or no direct sunlight. A base will need energy storage systems capable of supplying electricity and heat through extended darkness, alongside power generation that does not depend on sunlight. NASA is developing vertical solar arrays designed to collect sunlight near the lunar poles, as well as radioisotope power systems and small fission reactors. Nuclear fission could provide a particularly important source of continuous electricity, operating independently of solar conditions. NASA has announced plans for Lunar Reactor-1 to land on the surface in 2030. However, the reactor and the wider power distribution infrastructure still need to be developed and demonstrated for sustained operations. 2. Systems that extract water, oxygen, and fuel from lunar resources Transporting every kilogram (every pound) of water, oxygen, and propellant from Earth would make a permanent settlement extremely expensive. Instead, lunar infrastructure will need to use resources already present on the surface, a process known as in-situ resource utilization (ISRU). The lunar South Pole is particularly interesting because permanently shadowed craters may contain water ice. If engineers can locate, excavate, and process it at useful scales, the water could support drinking, hygiene, and life-support systems. It could also be separated into hydrogen and oxygen, potentially providing ingredients for rocket propellant. Oxygen may also be extracted from lunar soil , or regolith, which contains oxygen chemically bound in minerals. NASA researchers demonstrated an integrated solar-carbothermal prototype in 2026 that extracted oxygen from simulated lunar regolith. Scaling such systems for practical surface production remains a major challenge. 3. More autonomous life-support systems Astronauts cannot rely on a continuous supply of fresh air and water from Earth. A permanent base will need systems that recycle wastewater, remove carbon dioxide, control humidity, and maintain a breathable atmosphere with minimal human intervention. The International Space Station already uses an Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) that recovers approximately 90 percent of its water. It also removes carbon dioxide from cabin air and generates oxygen through water electrolysis. However, a lunar settlement will need more robust, maintainable systems that can operate for much longer periods with limited resupply. Equipment will need to handle failures, contamination, and changing crew requirements while allowing astronauts to repair or replace components. Recycling will also need to extend beyond water and air to include waste processing and, eventually, the recovery of useful materials. 4. Technology to keep lunar dust out of everything Lunar regolith is not ordinary terrestrial dust. Its particles are sharp, abrasive, and electrostatically charged, allowing them to cling to spacesuits, equipment, seals, solar panels, and optical surfaces. During Apollo, dust created problems for astronauts and hardware. At a permanent base, repeated exposure could damage mechanical joints, degrade equipment, contaminate habitats, and create health risks if particles enter the cabin. NASA has already demonstrated one promising approach. Its Electrodynamic Dust Shield uses electrical fields to move dust away from protected surfaces. The technology successfully removed lunar regolith from surfaces during Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1 in March 2025. However, a settlement will need a much broader dust-control system. This could include specialized spacesuit interfaces, airlocks, filters, dust-resistant seals, and cleaning equipment that can operate repeatedly without consuming large quantities of supplies. 5. Radiation shelters built into lunar habitats Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere protect people from much of the radiation arriving from space. The Moon has neither a substantial atmosphere nor a global magnetic field, leaving astronauts exposed to galactic cosmic rays and potentially dangerous solar particle events. A permanent habitat will therefore need more than a conventional pressurized structure. One solution is to cover living areas with thick layers of lunar regolith, creating shielding from radiation and micrometeorite impacts. NASA is investigating regolith-based protective structures and materials that could be manufactured using local resources. A base may also need a dedicated storm shelter where astronauts can spend periods of intense solar activity. The challenge is balancing protection with construction weight, available materials, and the need to maintain a safe, functional living environment. 6. Autonomous robots that can build the base Sending astronauts to construct roads, landing pads, berms, and habitat foundations would consume valuable mission time and expose crews to environmental hazards. Robotic construction systems could prepare much of the site before humans arrive. NASA is developing autonomous excavators such as its Infrastructure Pilot Excavator, designed to dig, collect, and transport lunar regolith for site preparation. Other research is exploring additive manufacturing, in which local material is processed into structural components or protective enclosures. These systems will need to work in reduced gravity, extreme temperatures, and abrasive dust while operating with limited supervision from Earth. Their ability to coordinate excavation, material handling, and construction will determine how quickly a lunar outpost can expand. 7. A lunar communications and navigation network A permanent Moon base will need reliable communications not only with Earth but also between astronauts, rovers, landers, orbiters, and other infrastructure. This is particularly important near the South Pole, where terrain can block direct radio links to Earth. NASA’s LunaNet framework aims to establish an internet-like communications and navigation architecture around the Moon. Lunar relay satellites could provide continuous connectivity in areas without a direct line of sight to Earth, while navigation services would help spacecraft and surface vehicles determine their positions without relying entirely on Earth-based tracking. In September 2026, NASA also awarded a contract to develop a lunar 5G communications system with integrated Wi-Fi 6. The planned demonstrations are intended to help establish a scalable surface network for future Moon Base operations. Building more than a place to land None of these technologies will be sufficient on its own. A permanent lunar settlement depends on power systems supporting life support, robots building infrastructure, local resources reducing dependence on Earth, and communications connecting it all. NASA’s phased Moon Base plan reflects this challenge. Initial missions are expected to test technologies and prepare the surface, followed by deployments of foundational infrastructure and eventually interconnected habitats. The goal is not simply to send people back to the Moon. It is to create an environment where they can remain, work, maintain their equipment, and expand their operations without depending on Earth for every essential resource. Achieving that will require a new generation of technologies designed to work together in an environment humans have only briefly explored.

title: US' 9,200-ton destroyer that fired dozens of missiles returns home
content: The U.S. Navy’s guided-missile destroyer USS Michael Murphy (DDG 112) has returned to Pearl Harbor after sailing more than 97,000 nautical miles during an 11-month deployment that placed it at the center of maritime security operations in the Middle East, the U.S. 3rd Fleet said in a statement.The homecoming sheds new light on the ship’s operational role during months of heightened tensions in the Persian Gulf, with the Navy revealing details of missions that had largely remained undisclosed while the deployment was underway.The destroyer returned to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on November 12 after operating across the U.S. 3rd, 5th and 7th Fleet areas of responsibility in support of what the Navy described as the “first naval blockade in 60 years.”According to the Navy, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer completed 12 contested transits through the Strait of Hormuz, escorted four merchant tankers to safety, coordinated the defense of 14 U.S. and coalition vessels, and launched dozens of Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles during Operation Epic Fury.Destroyer led maritime security operationsUSS Michael Murphy departed Pearl Harbor on December 1, 2025, as part of Carrier Strike Group 3 before entering the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility in late January. It later assumed the role of Surface Action Group Commander for Task Force 50, directing maritime security operations across the North Arabian Sea, Gulf of Oman and Strait of Hormuz.While in the conflict zone, its responsibilities extended well beyond escorting commercial shipping. The destroyer coordinated the protection of 14 U.S. and coalition vessels, including guided-missile destroyers, Littoral Combat Ships, six U.S. Coast Guard Fast Response Cutters and fleet replenishment oilers operating in contested waters.The 12 transits through the Strait of Hormuz stand out as one of the deployment’s defining achievements.According to the Navy, each passage took place under the threat of drones, missiles, fast attack craft, and naval mines while the destroyer escorted merchant tankers through one of the world’s most strategically important shipping lanes.“The Sailors of Michael Murphy demonstrated unmatched grit, professionalism, and warfighting excellence during this deployment,” said Cmdr. David Nicolas, commanding officer of Michael Murphy.“Whether defeating incoming air and surface threats or leading operations through contested choke points, this crew never hesitated. They answered every call of our nation, defended our allies, and lived up to the heroic namesake. I could not be prouder of this crew.”Capable of offensive and defensive strikesBuilt for multi-mission warfare, USS Michael Murphy combines long-range strike capability with layered air, surface and undersea defense. The warship can rapidly switch between offensive strike, fleet air defense and anti-submarine missions. The Mk 41 Vertical Launching System on the ship’s deck can fire Tomahawk cruise missiles to strike long-range land targets. The same launcher can be used for standard surface-to-air missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles for intercepting nearby aircraft and incoming missiles, and Vertical Launch Anti-Submarine Rockets that deliver torpedoes against hostile submarines.The destroyer can simultaneously detect, track, and engage multiple airborne and surface threats, supported by the its Aegis Weapon System integrated with the AN/SPY-1D(V) phased-array radar. The warship also carries a 5-inch Mk 45 naval gun, a Phalanx Close-In Weapon System for last-line defense against incoming missiles and drones, and two MH-60R Seahawk helicopters that extend its surveillance and anti-submarine reach far beyond the horizon.The Navy said these capabilities enabled USS Michael Murphy to launch dozens of Tomahawk strikes during Operation Epic Fury, as it continued to defend coalition forces and commercial shipping from aerial and maritime threats.​

title: Oceans absorbed 35% of fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions over 30 years
content: A new study published in the journal Science has provided some of the strongest evidence to date as to how Earth’s carbon sinks have changed over time.Researchers at UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography analyzed more than 30 years of atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements. According to the data, oceans absorbed 35 percent of fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions between 1990 and 2019, compared with 13 percent absorbed by land ecosystems. Together, the two sinks absorbed roughly half of those emissions. If lands and oceans weren’t absorbing half the CO₂ from fossil fuel emissions, “we would be living on a very different planet,” according to the study’s lead author Eric Morgan.“But these sinks can’t be observed directly. Figuring out exactly how much they have absorbed, and how they have changed over time, is a central goal of carbon cycle research,” Morgan told Phys.org.Ocean uptake increasedAccording to the study, oceans absorbed an average of 2.8 billion metric tons (3.1 billion US tons) of carbon dioxide per year between 1990 and 2019, about 35 percent of total fossil fuel emissions. Each decade, researchers observed that annual absorption increased by about 630 million metric tons (694 million US tons).Land ecosystems absorbed around 1.0 billion metric tons (1.1 billion US tons) of carbon dioxide a year, with an uncertainty of ±0.5 billion metric tons (0.55 billion US tons), far less than the oceans. The land sink peaked in the decade around 2009, and has declined ever since.“It was very surprising to see how the net land sink has not kept pace with rising CO₂ levels. Our data underscore that the land sink may be pretty fragile,” added Morgan.How researchers measured the sinksAs fossil fuels burn, they consume atmospheric oxygen and release carbon dioxide. On land, plants absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and release oxygen in the process. Ocean uptake, however, occurs primarily through reactions in seawater that do not affect oxygen levels. The researchers started their work by studying observations collected through the Scripps O₂ Program. By tracking changes in these gases, they estimated how much carbon entered the ocean and land ecosystems.The Scripps O₂ program was launched in 1989, it measures changes in atmospheric oxygen levels from air samples collected at stations along the Pacific from the high Arctic to the South Pole.“It is not easy to keep these kinds of measurements going year after year, but the payoff for improving our understanding of the carbon cycle is huge,” said co-author Ralph Keeling, who is also a professor at Scripps.Implications for climate modelsTheir findings challenge many climate models that simulate carbon uptake by land and oceans. Some of them have predicted that land uptake would increase. However, the data show that land sinks have not shifted that significantly. The amount of carbon they have absorbed has, in fact, declined.One theory points to deforestation and other land-use changes that may have released more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Now, thanks to this research, climate scientists might have to adjust climate models to accurately represent how land ecosystems absorb carbon.As for the major consequences of CO₂ emissions, Phys.org notes that ocean carbon sinks contribute to acidification. As the ocean absorbs more CO₂, the chemical reactions involved lower the pH of seawater, making it more acidic.Warmer waters hold less carbon dioxide than colder waters. As temperatures rise, the oceans might become less capable of absorbing carbon. Warmer surface water doesn’t mix with deeper, colder ocean water, which could be a long-term carbon storage facility that may no longer work.As the lead study author previously said, without these carbon sinks, “we would be living on a very different planet.” The latest research will hopefully equip scientists with the most up-to-date information about how the planet is dealing with the rising carbon dioxide levels.The study concludes that its observations question the ability of some process-based models to accurately predict future climate conditions.

title: US’ top rival’s jet drone that can strike beyond 500 miles intercepted
content: Ukraine has intercepted a Russian jet-powered Geran-5 attack drone in the Kyiv region using Sweden’s RBS-70 air defense system for the first time, according to Ukraine’s military. The interception highlights Kyiv’s efforts to counter faster Russian drones that are more difficult to engage than conventional propeller-driven attack UAVs.The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced on November 13 that personnel from the 1027th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment had destroyed the Geran-5 using the Swedish-made system. It did not disclose the precise location or time of the engagement.The regiment’s RBS-70 crew had described the interception in an earlier interview with Ukrainian outlet LB.ua, published on November 11. A commander identified by the callsign Vigo said the drone was traveling at more than 500 km/h (310 mph) and descended toward its target only a few minutes before impact, leaving air defense crews limited time to respond.Why the Geran-5 is harder to interceptUnlike the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones commonly associated with Russia’s Shahed-style attacks, the Geran-5 uses a turbojet engine and a conventional aircraft configuration. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) says the drone resembles Iran’s Karrar and incorporates components also found in other Russian Geran models.According to HUR’s January 2026 technical assessment, the Geran-5 has a maximum takeoff weight of approximately 850 kg (1,874 lb), a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h (280–373 mph), and an estimated range of up to 950 km (590 miles). These figures are Ukrainian intelligence estimates rather than independently verified performance measurements.Its higher speed reduces the time available for air defense crews to detect, identify, and engage it. That makes systems capable of tracking faster aerial targets increasingly important to Ukraine’s layered air defenses.How Sweden’s RBS-70 guided missile worksThe RBS-70, developed by Swedish defense company Saab, differs from many shoulder-fired air defense missiles that use infrared seekers to home in on an aircraft’s heat signature.Instead, it uses laser beam-riding guidance. The operator keeps the target within the system’s sight, while the missile follows a laser guidance corridor projected toward it. Because the missile does not rely on an infrared seeker, conventional heat-decoy flares are not an effective way to divert it.The system is also less vulnerable to certain forms of electronic jamming that can interfere with radar-guided weapons. However, its guidance method requires the operator to maintain a line of sight and track the target during the engagement.Depending on the missile variant, the RBS-70 family offers an engagement range of several kilometers. Saab’s newer RBS-70 NG configuration advertises a range exceeding 9 km (5.6 miles) and altitude coverage of up to 5 km (3.1 miles).Sweden continues to support Ukraine’s air defensesSweden has supplied Ukraine with RBS-70 systems as part of its military assistance. In February 2025, the Swedish government announced a SEK 1.2 billion ($113 million at the time) air-defense package that included procurement of the latest RBS-70 version and Tridon Mk2 anti-aircraft systems for Ukraine.The Geran-5 interception is not the first reported Ukrainian success against the jet-powered drone. In September 2026, Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment released footage of a Ukrainian-made STING interceptor drone destroying one.Ukraine has also been exploring other relatively affordable ways to counter faster aerial threats, including interceptor drones and automated machine-gun systems. The latest RBS-70 engagement demonstrates how established short-range missile systems can also contribute to that effort as Russia expands its use of jet-powered attack drones.

title: How the UK’s Aster 30 and US SM-6 compare in naval air defense
content: A destroyer’s air defenses can protect more than the ship carrying them. They can also shield nearby vessels from aircraft and incoming cruise missiles. That is the job shared by Europe’s Aster 30 and the US Navy’s Standard Missile-6, two ship-launched missiles built to defend fleets at sea.The Aster 30 grew out of cooperation among France, Italy, and the United Kingdom and now serves aboard Britain’s Type 45 destroyers. The US Navy fields the SM-6 aboard Aegis warships and uses it in a wider set of missions. The difference comes down to what each missile is designed to engage and how it fits into the ship carrying it.What each missile is designed to doBoth missiles provide what navies call area air defense. A ship equipped for that role can help defend a group of vessels, including ships with more limited air defenses of their own.Aircraft and cruise missiles are among the threats that Aster 30 and SM-6 are designed to intercept.The SM-6 also has a role in terminal ballistic missile defense. That means intercepting a ballistic missile during the final phase of its flight, as it approaches its target. Certain versions of the Aster 30 also have a ballistic missile defense role, so the comparison depends on which variant is under discussion. The clearest difference is at sea level. The US Navy also uses the SM-6 against surface targets, including ships. Aster 30’s development has centered on intercepting threats in the air.How the missiles fit into a warship’s defensesOn a British Type 45 destroyer, three names describe three different pieces of equipment. Sea Viper is the air-defense system, Aster 30 is the interceptor, and Sylver is the launcher that holds and fires it. The American equivalent brings together the Aegis combat system, the SM-6 missile, and the Mk 41 vertical launcher. The ship’s radar helps detect and track threats, while the launcher houses missiles in individual cells below deck.That distinction matters when a navy wants to carry a different missile. In 2026, the UK commissioned MBDA to study whether Aster 30 could launch from the US-built Mk 41.On Britain’s Type 45s, Aster 30 still launches from Sylver. If the study establishes that integration is feasible, it would give Britain another launcher design to consider for future warships.How the two missile families are evolvingThe Aster 30 name covers several versions. The B1 and B1NT variants reflect the European program’s push to expand its capabilities against ballistic missiles. That work spans land and sea. France and Italy are pursuing improved ballistic missile defense through the land-based SAMP/T NG system, while Britain is upgrading its shipboard defenses through Sea Viper Evolution. The capabilities a navy can field depend on the missile variant and the system it uses.The SM-6 has evolved through a series of block upgrades. Block I and Block IA are part of the existing family, while the US Navy has been developing Block IB to extend engagement range. The program’s history helps explain how the two missiles can share a purpose and still serve different roles. Europe’s Aster 30 upgrades have focused on widening the range of airborne and ballistic threats the interceptor can handle. The SM-6 grew from a fleet air-defense weapon into a missile the US Navy can also use for ballistic missile defense and against ships.

title: Researchers Have Discovered That a 6,000-Year-Old Clue to Ireland’s Farming History Was Completely Wrong
content:
Eurasian brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos). Credit: Malene Thyssen
Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.
For more than 30 years, the “Kerry Cow” helped shape a story about how farming reached Ireland. Bone fragments found on the coast of County Kerry appeared to show that domesticated cattle had arrived while the island’s inhabitants still lived by hunting and gathering. A new analysis has revealed that those supposed cattle were a bear and a wild boar.
The fragments were unearthed during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriter’s Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula. Dated to the end of Ireland’s Mesolithic period, which lasted from 8000 to 4000 BCE, they were considered the earliest evidence of domesticated farm animals in either Ireland or Britain.
Ferriter’s Cove is situated in the Dingle Peninsula, County Kerry, Ireland. Credit: Martin Moucheron
Their identification as cattle challenged existing theories about Ireland’s transition to farming, suggesting that its hunter-gatherers had established links with Neolithic farmers arriving from continental Europe before agriculture took hold on the island.
Bone proteins reveal bear and boar
Researchers led by Dr. Martin Moucheron at University College Dublin (UCD) returned to the original archaeological material, now stored at University College Cork (UCC). Working with Drs. Benjamin Gearey, Barra Ó Donnabháin, and Margaret McCarthy at UCC, and Kate Kanne at UCD, the team sent the bones to the CNRS laboratory in Lille, France.
Eurasian brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos). Credit: Charles James Sharp
There, the fragments underwent analysis using ZooMS, a technique that identifies animals through proteins preserved in ancient bone collagen, a structural component of bone. The results identified bear and wild boar rather than the domesticated cattle on which the earlier interpretation depended.
Ireland’s farming timeline loses a key clue
Reported in the latest edition of
, the newsletter of the
Prehistoric Society
, the findings remove a major piece of evidence from debates about when and how communities in Ireland and Britain moved from hunting and gathering to farming. There is currently no archaeological evidence supporting the idea that domesticated cattle, and by extension early farming communities, had reached or influenced Ireland before 4000 BCE. Losing that evidence does not establish a new arrival date, but it changes the basis for reconstructing that transition.
“Ferriter’s Cove is an iconic archaeological site, originally excavated by the Late Professor Peter Woodman, Department of Archaeology, UCC; this new collaboration with colleagues at UCD marks an exciting new phase of research and these remarkable results are set to change our understanding of the earliest evidence for agriculture in Ireland,” said Gearey.
The work is part of a Research Ireland-funded postdoctoral project at UCD’s School of Archaeology, led by Moucheron under the mentorship of Professor Graeme Warren. The project is reexamining important Mesolithic archaeological sites using modern scientific techniques.
Ferriter’s Cove is situated in the Dingle Peninsula, County Kerry, Ireland. Credit: Martin Moucheron
Warren added, “These exciting results show the real value in going back to key sites with new analytical techniques – which can change the stories we tell about our past”
“For at least four millennia hunting and gathering people lived on the island, and there is a common conception that they left little trace and that we know very little about them – unlike the megaliths of Neolithic farmers, who are portrayed in ways that feel very familiar in Ireland,” said Moucheron.
“But there is much we can understand about Mesolithic people just by going back to the sites and material we have, and by looking at them with new eyes and new techniques – and an open mind.”
Further analyses are underway to determine whether the bear remains belonged to brown bears or polar bears. The researchers hope this work will provide new insights into Ireland’s prehistoric bear populations before their extinction during the Bronze Age.

bone assemblage at Ferriter’s Cove, Co. Kerry, Ireland”

title: What Is Science, Really? Even Scientists Can’t Agree
content:
A new study reveals surprising differences in how scientists understand the purpose and practice of science, even among researchers working in the same field. Credit: Shutterstock
Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.
Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both? A study published in
Royal Society Open Science
found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science more than the general public does.
Study leader Marina Dubova, a former Santa Fe Institute postdoctoral researcher, is now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. Working with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu, she surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants evaluated 18 historical descriptions of science, including science as detective work, a search for truth, and a mirror reflecting reality.
Science seems more certain to the public
Scientists and the public generally agreed that science involves following curiosity and solving mysteries. The public tended to share an idealized picture of science as a reliable way to discover how the world works, placing less emphasis on creativity or uncertainty. That outlook could shape how people judge research and help explain their frustration when scientists cannot give firm answers or revise their conclusions as new evidence emerges.
The public’s views were closer to those of physicists and biologists than to those of researchers in psychology or the social sciences. One possible explanation, Dubova suggests, is that physics and biology feature more prominently in science education. More research is needed to test that connection.
The study found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Credit: Edson De la O / Santa Fe Institute
Same specialty, different ideas about science
Some scientists emphasized the search for objective truth, while others gave more weight to the judgment and creativity researchers bring to their work. They also disagreed about whether research follows established methods or requires improvisation. Few of the 18 descriptions received scientists’ full support, and they often had reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.
“What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield,” says Dubova. She suspects that researchers develop their approaches partly through experience, much as chefs develop different instincts about when to follow a recipe and when to improvise. Those differing conceptions of science could influence which discoveries researchers pursue.
AI could favor one vision of science
That diversity also raises a question for efforts to automate scientific research. As researchers develop artificial intelligence systems capable of conducting science, whose understanding of the work will those systems embody? Dubova worries that automation could reinforce one narrow conception of science at the expense of other valuable approaches.
For Dubova, the study is an early step toward understanding how these outlooks shape research itself. “Don’t take the common understanding of science for granted,” she says. “Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.”
Reference: “Everyone knows what science is…until you ask” by Marina Dubova and Qiawen E. Liu, 11 November 2026,
Royal Society Open Science

title: Scientists Just Challenged a 50-Year-Old Theory About How Evolution Works
content:
A new study challenges a long-standing evolutionary theory suggesting that essential genes receive special protection against mutations. Credit: Shutterstock
In bacteria and yeast, a gene’s importance did not predict its mutation rate, challenging the idea that evolution gives vital DNA preferential treatment.
Not all genes are equally important. Some are essential for survival, controlling basic functions such as copying DNA and keeping cells alive. Others can be lost with little or no effect. But does that mean evolution has found a way to shield its most vital genes from potentially harmful mutations?
For decades, scientists have debated whether essential genes are naturally less likely to mutate. Now, researchers at the
University of Bath
have put that idea to the test, with results that challenge a long-standing evolutionary hypothesis.
Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D. Hurst, from the university’s Centre for Evolution, examined spontaneous mutations in the bacterium
Escherichia coli
) and baker’s yeast (
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
). Their study, published November 12 in
PLOS Biology
, found no evidence that essential genes receive extra protection and offers a new explanation for why earlier research may have suggested otherwise.
The illusion of protected genes
“We’d expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them – what you can think of as ‘ghost mutations’,” Hurst said.
To reduce that problem, the team used data from “mutation accumulation” experiments designed to minimize the effects of natural selection. Three separate tests found no evidence that selection had substantially skewed the results.
“This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date,” Radrizzani said.
Essential genes showed no extra protection
The researchers compared mutation rates with experimental evidence showing what happens when individual genes are removed. Deleting an essential gene kills the cell, while losing other genes has little or no effect. This gave the team a way to test whether genes a cell depends on most were less likely to mutate.
“Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate,” Hurst said.
The team also assessed importance through the amount of a gene’s protein the cell produces and the strength of natural selection acting on the gene over evolutionary time.
“We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don’t have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate,” Radrizzani said.
A decades-old challenge to random mutation
These findings address a debate that began in 1972 and resurfaced as recently as 2023. At stake is the relationship between the two steps in the conventional account of evolution. Mutations first generate genetic variation. Natural selection and other forces then act on that variation, favoring some traits over others.
Darwin’s finches, which Charles Darwin encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835, offer a familiar example. Random mutations contribute to differences in beak size, allowing birds to use different food sources. When conditions favor particular foods, birds with beaks better suited to eating them are more likely to survive and reproduce. Their traits consequently become more common over generations.
The disputed proposal suggests that a gene’s importance also influences how often mutations arise in it. Vital genes would receive greater protection, while genes where change could help adaptation would mutate more frequently. Examples of the latter include genes in which mutations give bacteria antibiotic resistance or alter birds’ beak dimensions.
There is a theoretical difficulty with that proposal. Gene mutation rates are already so low that reducing them further for individual genes would offer very little benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.
“The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance,” said Radrizzani, who co-wrote the paper as part of her PhD. “It’s a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.”
Genes copied later during DNA replication did tend to mutate more frequently in the team’s analysis, showing that some features of the genome can help explain differences in mutation rates.
“While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm,” Hurst said.
Reference: “The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate” by Sofia Radrizzani and Laurence D. Hurst, 12 November 2026,
PLOS Biology

title: After 40 Years, Scientists Finally Detect Evidence of an Almost Impossible Particle Decay
content:
After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have detected evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that could offer new insights into the fundamental workings of matter. Credit: Stock
Evidence of a rare particle decay fits physics’ best theory, giving scientists a new way to test whether our understanding of matter leaves something out.
After more than 40 years of searching, physicists have found the first evidence of a particle decay predicted to occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The signal, recorded by the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC), offers a way to look for undiscovered particles through the influence they might have on that exceptionally unlikely event.
Inside the protons and neutrons at an atom’s center are smaller building blocks called up and down quarks. Beauty quarks are heavier members of the same family, produced in huge numbers when particles collide at the LHC, and they exist for only around one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying. LHCb studies particles containing these short-lived quarks. In the decay at the center of the new result, known as
Bd to mu mu
, one such particle transforms into two muons, particles similar to electrons but heavier.
With a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, the signal is strong enough to qualify as evidence of the decay, although more data will be needed to reach the five-sigma threshold required to claim a discovery in particle physics.
Professor Chris Parkes, head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, said, “This decay is remarkably unlikely, the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.”
Rare decays could reveal hidden particles
An undiscovered particle could change the chances of a beauty particle decaying in a particular way, giving physicists a means of detecting its influence even if they cannot observe it directly at the LHC. The rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to such effects. Researchers can therefore look for discrepancies between the measured decay rate and the predictions of the Standard Model, their best current theory of fundamental particles and their interactions. The new measurement matches those predictions, and greater precision could help reveal where the theory might eventually begin to break down.
LHCB. Credit CERN
Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, deputy physics coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, said, “There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.
“The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.”
Pinpointing where beauty particles decay
Just five millimeters, or about 0.2 inches, from the LHC beams sits the Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector that tracks the paths of particles emerging from collisions with extreme precision. This major UK-built component is part of the upgraded LHCb experiment. University of Manchester researchers played key roles in the experiment and its upgrade, including developing detector technology that helped make the measurement possible.
Dr. Stefano De Capua, who led construction of the detectors at the University of Manchester, said, “We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.”
Parkes led the international LHCb collaboration through construction of the upgrade and led its approval of the new result. Made a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year for his work on LHCb, he said, “The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking – a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.
“The UK made the largest nation contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today’s result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start, we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.”
Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who was not involved in the experiment, said, “This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don’t understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing – that’s science! LHCb is a major scientific success.”
The experiment is funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council as part of UK Research and Innovation.

title: “A Magnetar Is Born”: Supercomputer Simulates One of the Universe’s Most Violent Collisions
content:
A magnetar is a rare type of neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field, up to 1,000 times stronger than that of a typical neutron star and trillions of times stronger than Earth’s. Credit: Shutterstock
A black hole isn’t the only possible outcome when neutron stars collide: simulations suggest some mergers can create the extreme magnetic fields of magnetars in milliseconds.
When two neutron stars collide, the result is often a black hole. But some mergers leave behind a massive neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field. New supercomputer simulations suggest that these collisions can produce magnetar-strength magnetic fields in just milliseconds, offering a possible explanation for how some of the universe’s most magnetic objects form.
Magnetars are a rare class of neutron stars, distinguished by magnetic fields that can be roughly 1,000 times stronger than those of ordinary neutron stars. They are associated with intense bursts of radiation, including soft gamma-ray repeaters, and may also produce some fast radio bursts.
Simulating a Neutron Star Collision in Extraordinary Detail
Using Japan’s FUGAKU supercomputer, researchers simulated the collision of two neutron stars, each with 1.35 times the Sun’s mass. The calculation achieved a spatial resolution of 6.25 meters (20.5 feet), allowing the team to track small-scale turbulence and its effects on magnetic fields throughout the merger.
The stars initially had magnetic fields of approximately 3.16 trillion gauss, consistent with the upper range observed in binary pulsars. The collision generated fields reaching around 10 quadrillion gauss across parts of the remnant, with localized regions reaching even greater strengths.
The researchers say the simulation demonstrates that “the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability that emerges when the two neutron stars touch amplifies the magnetic field to an expected electromagnetic saturation energy of ∼ 10⁵⁰ erg within 3 ms after the merger.”
How Turbulence Amplifies Magnetic Fields
The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability develops when neighboring layers of fluid move at different velocities. During a neutron star merger, enormous differences in fluid motion generate turbulence that stretches and strengthens magnetic fields.
Initially, the strongest amplification occurs on very small scales. The turbulent magnetic field subsequently influences progressively larger regions of the merged star, allowing magnetic amplification to reach stellar scales.
The researchers say the instability “induces stellar-scale magnetic field amplification by at least a factor of 316.”
Within approximately five milliseconds, the simulated stellar-scale magnetic field had increased from 3.16 trillion gauss to around one quadrillion gauss, reaching magnetar strength. As the researchers put it, “Namely, a magnetar is born.”
Could These Newborn Magnetars Survive?
Although the simulation produced magnetar-strength fields, the researchers caution that uncertainties in how turbulence and magnetic dissipation operate at extremely small scales could affect the estimated amplification.
In one extrapolation to more realistic conditions, the simulated stellar-scale field could be overestimated by a factor of 10. Even under that assumption, the resulting magnetic field would still reach approximately 100 trillion gauss.
The magnetic structure also remained concentrated near the remnant’s equatorial plane rather than forming the organized polar field associated with launching relativistic jets. Additional magnetic processes, particularly the magnetorotational instability, may be needed to develop that configuration.
The researchers say their “result suggests that a magnetar formation could be inevitable in binary neutron star mergers at least temporarily following the mergers, unless it promptly collapses to a black hole.”
The simulations cover only the earliest moments after the collision. Longer calculations will be needed to determine how these magnetic fields evolve, whether they help power energetic outbursts, and how long the resulting neutron star can survive before potentially collapsing into a black hole.
Reference: “A magnetar formation in binary neutron star merger” by Kenta Kiuchi, Alexis Reboul-Salze, Yuichiro Sekiguchi and Masaru Shibata, June 9, 2026,

title: Researchers Turn Moon Dust Into LEGO-Like Bricks That Could Build Future Lunar Bases
content:
Future Moon bases could provide astronauts with places to live, work, and conduct scientific research while supporting long-term lunar exploration. Scientists are developing innovative ways to build these outposts using materials found on the Moon, potentially reducing the need for costly supplies from Earth. Credit: Shutterstock
Building on the Moon could require fewer supplies from Earth, as scientists have found a way to fuse simulated lunar dust into interlocking bricks without added materials.
Building a future home on the Moon might someday resemble assembling a giant LEGO set. Instead of plastic pieces, astronauts could use interlocking bricks made from lunar dust, creating structures from materials already available on the Moon’s surface.
Researchers at the
University of Arkansas
have taken an early step toward that possibility by demonstrating that simulated lunar dust can be 3D-printed into LEGO-like building blocks without adding other materials. The approach could reduce the construction supplies NASA would need to transport from Earth as it works toward establishing permanent settlements on the Moon.
The key ingredient is lunar regolith, the loose, dusty material covering the Moon’s surface. Unlike soil on Earth, regolith contains no organic matter. It consists of jagged particles formed over billions of years as asteroids, micrometeorites, and other space debris struck the Moon.
For their experiments, the researchers used Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercially available material designed to imitate samples collected during the Apollo missions in the 1960s and early 1970s.
The study, published in the journal
NPJ Advanced Manufacturing
, was led by first author Cole McCallum, then an undergraduate at the University of Arkansas, and senior author Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering.
Lunar dust bonds without added ingredients
To create the bricks, the team used a 3D-printing technique called laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source, such as a laser, heats selected portions of the powder, causing the particles to bond together through a process known as sintering. The printing bed then lowers, allowing another layer of powder to be added. Repeating these steps gradually builds a three-dimensional object.
Other researchers have successfully printed objects using lunar regolith mixed with binding agents. However, those additional ingredients would have to be transported from Earth, increasing the amount of material needed for construction on the Moon.
A 3D printer was used to create stackable bricks of pure lunar dust. Credit: Cole McCallum
The Arkansas team demonstrated for the first time that simulated lunar regolith could be sintered directly into reconfigurable construction blocks without a binder, using a relatively low-power light source.
“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said.
The researchers produced blocks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. These shapes could fit together much like LEGO bricks, allowing individual pieces to be assembled into larger structures.
Lunar bricks still face a strength problem
Although the researchers successfully created interlocking blocks, the material is not yet strong enough for all the demands of lunar construction. Bricks made entirely from simulated regolith were more porous and structurally weaker than objects printed with binding agents.
“These structures we’re making can be self-supported,” McCallum said. “But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet.”
The team must also determine how the printing process would behave under actual lunar conditions. According to Shou, further experiments are needed to understand its performance in microgravity and vacuum environments, while improvements to the bricks’ mechanical properties will be necessary before they become practical construction materials.
Shou remains optimistic that the approach could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture components and structures for permanent settlements on the Moon.
For McCallum, the project also marked an important early step in his scientific career. A native of Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou’s laboratory early in his undergraduate studies, encouraged by his professor’s commitment to involving students in research.
“He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research,” McCallum said.
McCallum graduated in May with degrees in mechanical engineering and physics. He was subsequently awarded an inaugural Lafayette Fellowship, a program established to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the United States. Only 30 fellows were selected from more than 3,400 applicants to pursue master’s degrees in France.
He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-SUPAERO), one of France’s leading aerospace engineering schools.
Although his academic focus has shifted away from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou’s laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with teaching him how to navigate the challenges of scientific investigation.
“It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through,” he said. “It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.”
Reference: “Additive manufacturing of lunar regolith for reconfigurable building blocks toward lunar habitation” by Cole McCallum, Youwen Liang, Nahid Tushar, Ben Xu, Bo Zhao, Hao Zeng and Wan Shou, 29 August 2026,
npj Advanced Manufacturing
DOI: 10.1038/s44334-026-00111-x
